# Deployment runbook: data-download

# Generated by genproj (docker-container capability, registry=ghcr.io,

# network mode=bridge, watchtower=false, homepage=true)

# NOTE: watchtower was generated off, then switched on for the host on

# 2026-11-12 via the scope=nick label — see §3. Re-running genproj will not

# restore that; it is a host-side label.

## 1. Build & publish the image

The repository's Buildkite pipeline (`.buildkite/pipeline.yml`) contains a
`docker_publish` step that builds the image for `linux/amd64` and
pushes it to `ghcr.io/nickbrett1/data-download` on every push to `main` (tagged with the commit
SHA and `latest`).

Builds use a **registry-backed BuildKit cache**: each `docker_publish` run
pulls the previous layer cache from the `:buildcache` tag
(`ghcr.io/nickbrett1/data-download:buildcache`) and
pushes it back with `mode=max`, so only changed layers rebuild. The first run
after enabling seeds the cache (still cold — same duration as before); the
speedup shows from the **second** run. The `:buildcache` tag is a cache-only
artifact and is never used as a deployable image.

- The registry namespace (`nickbrett1`) is derived from the
  authenticated GitHub identity at generation time.
- Registry credentials are resolved at run time from Doppler
  (`common`/`prd`, secret `GHCR_UPDATE_TOKEN`) using the `DOPPLER_TOKEN` the
  agent's `environment` hook provides:
  - `GHCR_USERNAME` — the GHCR namespace the image is published under
  - the resolved `GHCR_UPDATE_TOKEN` — a **classic** PAT with the
    `write:packages` scope, used to push to GHCR
- **Package visibility** defaults to `public` (so the NAS/Watchtower can pull
  with **no credentials**). The generated Dockerfile carries
  `org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/nickbrett1/data-download`,
  so GHCR links the published package to this repo on first push — a **public
  repo yields a public package** automatically. To keep a package private, keep
  the repo private (or set `imageVisibility: private` in the genproj config;
  then `docker login` is required on the NAS — see section 3).

### One-time CI setup (agent `environment` hook)

Before the first push can publish an image, the agent must supply the registry
credentials:

1. In the agent's `environment` hook, export `DOPPLER_TOKEN` so the
   `docker_publish` step can read `GHCR_UPDATE_TOKEN` from Doppler
   (`common`/`prd`) at run time.
2. Confirm `plugins-path` is set in `buildkite-agent.cfg` — every step here
   uses a plugin, and agent v4 has no usable default.

The registry token never lands in the agent's `environment` hook, where
every job on the fleet could read it. See `.buildkite/README.md` for the full list of agent
prerequisites.

> GitHub **fine-grained** PATs cannot access the Container registry (GHCR)
> yet, and offer no "Packages: read & write" permission — do not use one here.

## 2. Deploy on the NAS (Synology Container Manager)

1. Open Container Manager -> Project -> Create.
2. Point it at this repository (or copy `docker-compose.yml` + `.env` to the NAS).
3. Set environment variables in a `.env` next to the compose file (see `.env.example`).
4. Start the project.

For non-Synology hosts: `docker compose up -d`.



## 3. Auto-updates with Watchtower (poll model)

Watchtower polls the registry and recreates the container when the image digest
changes — no inbound ports from CI are required.

**Status: enabled** (owner decision, 2026-11-12; this reverses an earlier
deliberate exclusion that was in place while the service was read-only).

- On `ryzen`, the container joins `watchtower-nick` via
  `com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.scope=nick`. That instance runs with
  `WATCHTOWER_SCOPE=nick`, a 60 s poll, and `WATCHTOWER_CLEANUP=true`, and it
  only considers containers carrying the same scope label — so the label is the
  whole opt-in, and the `...watchtower.enable=true` form is not used here.
- **Consequence, accepted:** a green build on `main` reaches the host
  unattended within about a minute of the image changing. Tests and the linter
  gate that, not a human.
- Watchtower recreates the container from its existing config, so the
  `homepage.*` labels, the mem limits and the `/srv/appdata/data-download`
  volume all survive a roll.
- Reconsider this before any phase that gives the service spending authority:
  unattended roll-forward and unattended money are different risk classes.
- **Public packages**: no credentials needed on the host.
- **Private packages**: `docker login ghcr.io` on the host once
  (Watchtower uses the Docker daemon's credentials).

## 4. Rolling back a bad update

Watchtower recreates the container on every push to `main`, so a broken build
can reach the NAS. Every image is also tagged with its commit SHA, so you can
pin the compose file to a known-good build while you fix the repo:

1. Find the SHA of the last good commit (e.g. the GHCR package page, or
   `git log` on your machine).
2. In `docker-compose.yml`, change the image to the pinned SHA:
   `image: ghcr.io/nickbrett1/data-download:<commit-sha>`
3. Restart the project (`docker compose up -d`, or restart it in Container
   Manager).

Watchtower watches the tag referenced by the compose file, so a pinned SHA tag
will not be overwritten until you move the image back to `latest`.

## 5. Homepage dashboard

Append `deploy/homepage-services.yaml` to your Homepage `services.yaml`
(and enable the `homepage` Docker provider) to show a health widget for the
service.

**Point the `href` at the serve URL.** `https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net/`, not
`http://<host>:8820/`. The host-and-port link does not work at all any more:
§6 publishes the port on loopback only, so `http://<host>:8820/` is refused from
every other machine, and only `tailscale serve` can reach the app. The widget
URL stays on loopback — Homepage is server-side on the host, so
`http://localhost:8820/healthz` reaches the published port, and `/healthz` needs
no identity.

**Never put a token in `href`.** Reading needs no credential: the UI is a
public read-only projection (see the main README, "What is public, and what is
not"). A `homepage.href=?token=…` would write a live credential into a Docker
label, the compose file, and every proxy log and screenshot of the dashboard —
and since nothing on the read path uses tokens, it would buy nothing.

## 6. Approving a request

Approving spends money, so it is the one verb the UI offers — and it is
authorised by **who you are**, not by a secret. `tailscale serve` terminates the
tailnet connection on this host and proxies to the container on loopback,
adding `Tailscale-User-Login` for the peer it just authenticated. The app trusts
that header only from a loopback peer, then checks the login against
`DATA_DOWNLOAD_APPROVERS`.

That means two things have to be true, and both are a line of config.

**Serve is the only thing that reaches the container.** The check is the *peer
address*, and the trust is only as good as the claim that nothing else can
manufacture that address. So the port is published on loopback and nothing else:

```yaml
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8820:8820"
```

**Do not "fix" this to `0.0.0.0` to make a host-and-port link work.** That was
tried, and it re-opened approval completely. Published on all interfaces, the
port also listens on the tailnet interface, and a connection to any address that
is *local to the host* — the node's tailnet IP, its LAN IP — is re-originated by
Docker's port forward and reaches the container from the bridge gateway. It then
arrives looking exactly like the Serve hop, and the gateway is trusted. Measured
on the real deployment, from another tailnet member with no `tailscale serve`
anywhere in the path:

```bash
NODE_IP=$(tailscale ip -4 ryzen)
curl -H "Tailscale-User-Login: you@example.com" "http://$NODE_IP:8820/v1/whoami"
# -> HTTP 200 {"login":"you@example.com","approver":true}
```

Anyone on the tailnet could approve spend as anyone else. Loopback binding cuts
it at the socket: there is no listener to accept the forged header, and the
connection is refused before HTTP exists. The cost is that the read projection
is only reachable through Serve too — no more `http://<host>:8820/` from the
LAN. That is the intended trade; a public read view is not worth a forgeable
approval.

**Your login is named in the allowlist** — in `.env` beside the compose file:

```bash
DATA_DOWNLOAD_APPROVERS="you@example.com"
```

Then have Serve front it, and apply the env — **`--force-recreate`, not a
restart**: watchtower and `docker restart` reuse the container's existing config
and will not re-read `.env`.

```bash
sudo tailscale serve --bg 8820          # https://<nas>.<tailnet>.ts.net → 127.0.0.1:8820
sudo tailscale serve status
docker compose up -d --force-recreate
```

Open a request at the serve URL. The card names the login Serve asserted and
offers one button; approving is two clicks with the ceiling between them, and
the record shows a `human` event with that login as the actor, the job hash and
`via: serve`.

### When it refuses: read the peer it names

Every refusal carries the address the request arrived from, because there are
three different hops that can go wrong and only one of them is a setting.

| what the page says | what is actually wrong |
| --- | --- |
| `no Tailscale-User-Login header: this request arrived from 172.18.0.1 directly` | the request reached the container through the host's port forward with no Serve in front of it — a `curl` on the host itself, or an old bookmark that has not started failing yet. Open the serve URL instead. Being *on* the tailnet adds nothing: the header comes from `tailscale serve`, not from the network |
| `a Tailscale-User-Login header arrived from 172.17.0.1, which is not a hop this service trusts` | Serve is working, but Docker's port forward re-originated the connection: the container sees the bridge gateway, not loopback. Add that address to `DATA_DOWNLOAD_TRUSTED_PROXIES` |
| `this tailnet login is not named in DATA_DOWNLOAD_APPROVERS` | both hops are fine; the login is not on the allowlist |

The middle case is the container tax and the reason the setting exists. Serve on
the host connects to `127.0.0.1:8820`; Docker forwards that into the container
from the bridge gateway, so "loopback" is no longer the peer. Two ways to deal
with it:

```bash
# 1. name the gateway the refusal printed
DATA_DOWNLOAD_TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.17.0.1

# 2. or take the container out of the path
#    (network_mode: host, so Serve's connection really is loopback)
```

Option 1 only holds while the port is bound to loopback — see above. The trust
in the gateway address is the trust in "the only path that produces that peer
is the host's own port forward", and publishing on `0.0.0.0` breaks that
sentence.

`DATA_DOWNLOAD_APPROVERS` unset means **nobody** may approve: the door fails
closed rather than treating "has a tailnet" as "may spend". Funnel (public)
traffic carries no identity header at all, so approval cannot work over Funnel
by construction.

**What the allowlist cannot tell you: `approver` is per *login*, not per device.**
`tailscale serve` reports the login that owns the node, so every node registered
to the same person presents the same value — a laptop, a phone, a build box, and
an unattended agent all read as `approver: true`. On a single-user tailnet that
is the honest description of who may spend. If the tailnet ever grows a second
human or a shared device, the allowlist is not the mechanism that separates
them: use a per-user login, and remember that tagged devices carry no login at
all (so they can never approve).

The old `approve` token and the `;…:approve` entry in
`DATA_DOWNLOAD_API_TOKENS` are gone from this file: the scope is still accepted
so an existing `.env` starts, it logs a warning, and it gates nothing. Delete it
when you next touch the file.

### The CLI, when the UI is not the tool you want

A shell on the host is still a door — a local one, with no route and no
identity, which is exactly why it is not the default:

```bash
docker exec -it data-download python -m data_download.approve \
  <request_id> --actor nick --note "cheap window"
```

### Running an approved request (phase 5)

An approved row is a queue entry, not a download. One command runs one:

```bash
docker exec -it data-download python -m data_download.runner <request_id>
docker exec -it data-download python -m data_download.runner --next
```

The bytes land in
`<DATA_DOWNLOAD_DATASETS_DIR>/<vendor>/<dataset>/<request_id>/files/` (so
`/srv/datasets/databento/GLBX.MDP3/...` here),
which is `/datasets` in the container and a shared directory on the host
(`DATA_DOWNLOAD_DATASETS_HOST_DIR`: `/srv/datasets` on ryzen; a `/volume1` share
on a Synology). Create the host directory first: Docker will create a missing
bind source as root-owned, which is usually not what the share wants.

**The driver is a stub.** It writes placeholder files that begin `STUB:`, makes
no network call and cannot spend. The run is real in every other respect — the
claim, the lease, the verdict, the `landed_sha256`, the `landed` event — which
is the point: the first real download should not also be the first test of the
settlement path. Do not read a `succeeded` row as data until the driver says
`DatabentoDriver` in `landing.json`.

If the runner dies mid-run the row stays `running` until the lease expires
(900 s), then `v_stuck` reports `lease_expired` and the next claim reclaims it.
There is no sweeper, and no second mechanism: the reclaim is the same CAS.

## 7. Networking notes

- Network mode is `bridge`.
- External networks: this service joins `ai_proxy`, created and managed outside this compose file (genproj emits `networks: { <name>: { external: true } }`). Sibling containers reach it by container name on that network.
- `docker-compose.yml` is generated: a `networks` block added by hand is overwritten on regeneration. Declare external networks with the `externalNetworks` configuration instead.
- If your container needs fixed UDP ports or multicast (e.g. LAN protocols like
  Govee), set `networkMode: host` in the genproj configuration — bridge mode
  cannot pass multicast and fixed low ports reliably.
- Only one LAN-protocol client may bind the fixed ports per host IP.
- For private services (Tailscale-only), set `publishPort` to
  `127.0.0.1:<port>:<port>` so the port is not exposed on the LAN.
- Homepage href/widget URLs use the **published host port** (the left-hand
  side of `publishPort`), so `127.0.0.1:3002:3000` produces
  `http://<hostname>:3002/` — never the container port.

## 8. Data mounts

Configure `dataMounts` in the genproj configuration to mount host directories
into the container, e.g. `[{ "hostPath": "/volume1/marketdata", "containerPath": "/data", "readOnly": true }]`.
They are emitted into the compose `volumes:` section (read-only by default).

## 9. Healthchecks, env vars and system packages

All three are config-driven on the `docker-container` capability — the
generated Dockerfile, compose file and Homepage widget stay consistent:

- `healthcheck`: `none` (default for Python), `http:<path>` (e.g.
  `http:/healthz`; installs `curl` on Python images), or `command:<cmd>`.
  The Homepage widget is only emitted when a real health endpoint exists.
- `healthcheckTimeout`: the Docker `HEALTHCHECK --timeout` as a duration string
  (e.g. `"10s"`). Defaults are split by probe type: `10s` for an `http:<path>`
  check (the app does real work behind the request), `3s` for a `command:<cmd>`
  check. Raise it if your health endpoint is slow rather than editing the
  generated Dockerfile.
- `envVars`: emitted into the compose `environment:` and `.env.example`
  (e.g. `["MCP_PORT=3001"]`). Compose entries use `${KEY:-default}`
  interpolation so a NAS-side `.env` can override them.
- `pythonDependencies`: runtime Python deps emitted into `[project]`
  dependencies of `pyproject.toml` (e.g. `["mcp>=1.2.0", "mcpo>=0.0.20",
"httpx>=0.27.0"]`). Pin only versions that exist on PyPI: the editable install
  runs before lint/test, so an unsatisfiable specifier fails the build on its
  first command.
- `aptPackages`: Debian packages installed in the runtime image via apt
  (e.g. `["iproute2", "curl"]`).
- `command` / `entrypoint`: override the container CMD/ENTRYPOINT (exec form,
  e.g. `"command": ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]`). When the value points at
  `/usr/local/bin/<script>`, genproj copies `scripts/<script>` from your repo
  into the image (chmod +x) — keep the script in `scripts/`.

Regenerate with `overwrite: true` to apply these to an existing repo — existing
app code is preserved; only generated infra files are updated.

### The MCP endpoint (`/mcp`)

Same container, no extra service: the app mounts an MCP server at `/mcp`, so
the URL a client is given is `https://<node>.<tailnet>.ts.net/mcp/` (streamable
HTTP). It is reachable wherever the app is — the tailnet, via `tailscale serve`.

One setting, on the **app** service:

```
DATA_DOWNLOAD_MCP_TOKEN=<one of the tokens already in DATA_DOWNLOAD_API_TOKENS>
```

The value must be a token from `DATA_DOWNLOAD_API_TOKENS`: the tools
authenticate through `/v1` like any other caller, so the scopes that token has
are what the surface can do. `submit+read` lets an agent file requests and read
the book; `read` alone is a status surface. Unset (or a value that is not in the
list) means `/mcp` is not mounted — `404`, with one log line at boot naming the
setting — and everything else is unaffected. No value of this setting can
approve: approval stays the page's two clicks and the tailnet identity behind
them.

Register it **once** in the MCP hub and assign that one registration to every
consumer (the data group for status, the sourcing agent for filing). Two
registrations of the same URL drift: one gets the token rotated and the other
stops working months later. The tool list is in the main README, "The MCP
surface".

## 10. The driver queue (a missing driver gets built)

Phase 5.5. When an approved request's vendor has no installed driver, the runner
does **not** fail the request: it leaves the row `approved`, notes
`driver_state`, and enqueues one `driver_jobs` row for that vendor (the partial
unique index means ten requests for one missing driver are one job). The driver
worker works that queue:

```
queued -> building -> gated -> probing -> merging -> installing -> installed
              \-> needs_human        (a stop, never a retry loop)
```

### Three containers, and who owns what

| container | owns |
|---|---|
| `data-download` (the control plane) | the store, **both** queues, the pages, the demand signal, the forge: gate, changed paths, merge, PR |
| `data-download-drivers` | executes driver code, **owns and writes `/drivers`**, downloads data |
| `openhands` | authors a driver in a conversation, on a branch, and pushes it |

The rule behind that table is one sentence: **the process that runs the code
owns the directory it runs from.** So the app's `/drivers` mount is read-only,
and installation is a POST of the merged tree to the runtime
(`POST /v1/drivers/install`, bearer token), which writes it atomically and picks
it up on the next request because discovery re-globs on every request. The app
never needs the volume writable, and the runtime never needs GitHub egress or a
forge token.

That also removed the host loop, which existed for two reasons that are both
gone or inverted:

- *The app image has no `git`/`gh`.* It does not need them: the agent does the
  git, and the app asks the forge over HTTPS with `github_api`.
- *The installer needed the drivers volume writable.* It no longer writes there.

The other half of that rule is on the drivers side: its own `/drivers` mount
must be **read-write**, because it is the thing that writes there. A composed
`:ro` mount refuses every install with `install_refused`, and the symptom is
nothing more dramatic than a merged driver that never appears in
`GET /v1/drivers`. The reason lives beside the mount in that repository's
`docker-compose.yml`, and in its deployment runbook.

`driver_build` is still one job, walked as far as it can go, and still exits
`--once` from the command line for a manual run. What changed is the thing that
calls it: `driver_build.DriverWorker`, an asyncio task started by the app's
lifespan next to the request `Worker`, with the same properties -- it never
sleeps while there is work, it is nudged by an approval, and every step runs in
a worker thread so an authoring conversation that lasts tens of minutes does not
block the pages.

### What the app needs

All of this is on the **app** service. Environment, in `/srv/docker/data-download/.env`:

```
DATA_DOWNLOAD_GITHUB_TOKEN=<a token that can read checks and merge on the drivers repo>
DATA_DOWNLOAD_DRIVER_REPO=nickbrett1/data-download-drivers
DATA_DOWNLOAD_DRIVER_BASE=main
DATA_DOWNLOAD_DRIVER_JOBS=on
DATA_DOWNLOAD_DRIVER_JOBS_INTERVAL=60
DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_URL=http://openhands:8000
DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_WORKDIR=/projects/driver-loop
DATA_DOWNLOAD_AUTHOR_TIMEOUT=3600
DATA_DOWNLOAD_AUTHOR_BUDGET=2.00
DATA_DOWNLOAD_AUTHOR_ITERATIONS=200
```

**The URL is a container name on the agent server's own port, and both halves
of that matter.** The canvas publishes `8000/tcp` on the host as `3088`, so
`http://openhands:3088` can never work from another container -- it fails with
`ECONNREFUSED`, which reads like the agent being down. `openhands:8000` works
because both containers are on `ai_proxy`. `http://ryzen:3088` (the host
publish, through the LAN or the tailnet) also works, but only as long as that
name resolves; it is the fallback, not the deployment.

Plus two mounts, because the app container has **no docker CLI and no docker
socket** -- and should not have one:

```yaml
    volumes:
      - /srv/docker/openhands/projects:/projects
      - /srv/docker/openhands/data/agent-canvas/api-key.txt:/run/openhands/api-key.txt:ro
    environment:
      DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_PROJECTS_DIR: /projects
      DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_KEY_FILE: /run/openhands/api-key.txt
```

- **The key file** is what the agent server generated on first boot. Mounting it
  is how the control plane authenticates without `docker exec`; a recreated
  container has a new key, and a mounted file follows it.
- **`/projects`** is the agent's workspace, mounted here **at the same path the
  agent sees it**. That is the whole credential handoff: the harness writes
  `0600` `push-credential` into the branch's workspace directory before the
  conversation starts and removes it afterwards (plus a stale sweep at the start
  of every run, because `finally` does not run on SIGKILL). Same path on both
  sides means the prompt's path is *the* path -- nothing is translated, and a
  mount at a different path is refused by name.

- **The uid matters, and it is the failure that looks like nothing.** This image
  declares no `USER`, so it runs as root and writes the credential root-owned.
  The agent runs as `uid 10001` in its own container: a `0600` root-owned file,
  inside a `0700` root-owned directory, is a credential it cannot open and a
  path it cannot even enter -- with no error anywhere, just an agent that
  silently pushes nothing. So the workspace hands the file *and* the directories
  leading to it to `DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_AGENT_UID:GID` (default
  `10001:10001`) whenever this process is root. A host run is already the same
  user and does nothing.

On the OpenHands side, `/projects` must therefore be a **bind mount**, not the
anonymous volume it is today:

```yaml
    volumes:
      - /srv/docker/openhands/projects:/projects
```

Careful: `/projects` is not declared in the OpenHands compose at all -- it comes
from the image's `VOLUME /projects` instruction, so Docker minted an
**anonymous** volume (`docker inspect openhands` shows `"anonymous": ""`, no
`com.docker.compose.volume` label) and has been re-attaching that same one
across container recreations. Adding a bind changes the mount, and the volume's
contents do not follow it. Convert in this order:

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /srv/docker/openhands/projects
sudo chown 10001:10001 /srv/docker/openhands/projects
docker run --rm -v 2019ba8c…:/from -v /srv/docker/openhands/projects:/to \
  alpine sh -c 'cp -a /from/. /to/ && ls -A /to | wc -l'
# then add the bind to the compose file and `docker compose up -d`
```

The app cannot see an anonymous volume, so leaving it as one means no authoring.

Verified on ryzen 2026-11-25: the volume held three entries, all three were
copied, `/projects` now reports `"Type":"bind"` with source
`/srv/docker/openhands/projects`, and the agent's API key survived the
recreation because it lives in the `./data` bind rather than the volume.

**Two ownership facts that the deployment depends on, both load-bearing:**

- the key file is `0600 10001:10001` inside a `0700` directory, so only a
  **root** reader gets it -- which the app is, currently. Give that image a
  `USER` and this mount stops working.
- `/projects/driver-loop` is `0700` because it was made by the agent. It works
  only because the app is root; a non-root app could not read the job
  directories at all. If the app is ever dropped to a uid, that tree needs a
  group both containers share.

### The deployed compose drifts from this repository's, deliberately

`/srv/docker/data-download/compose.yaml` is not a copy of `docker-compose.yml`
and must not be synced wholesale. On 2026-11-25 it differed in six ways that
matter: the Homepage tile (`Data & Markets`, `mdi-database-arrow-down`,
weight 150 -- all owner-set), the `data-download-internal` network declaration,
`mem_limit`/`mem_swap_limit`, `name:`, the `x-logging` anchor, and the header
comments. Only the `app` service's `environment:` and `volumes:` are meant to
track this repository; everything else is local.

### What the loop will not do

- **It does not merge what it was not allowed to merge.** Every changed path in
  the pushed commit must be under `drivers/` or `tests/fixtures/`, read from
  GitHub's own diff. One file outside and the job stops for a human.
- **It does not trust its own gate.** Green means every check run is complete and
  in `success`/`neutral`/`skipped`; no check runs at all is *not* green.
- **It does not overwrite an installed version it did not make.** The runtime
  refuses a version that already exists unless the request carries the digest it
  installed last time; a directory a person installed has a digest this job has
  never recorded and stays refused.
- **It does not probe for free.** The probe is the triggering request's own Job,
  shrunk to one symbol and one day, priced *before* `submit` and refused if it
  would exceed `PROBE_BUDGET_USD` ($1).

### Watching it

There is no unit and no log file: it is the app's own log.

```
docker logs -f data-download            # or journalctl -u data-download
sqlite3 /srv/appdata/data-download/data-download.db \
  "select id, vendor, state, attempts, last_error from driver_jobs order by created_at desc"
```

A row in `needs_human` is the loop saying it stopped; `last_error` names the step.
Nothing retries it — clear or fix the cause and re-enqueue.

The authoring conversation itself is worth reading in the canvas
(`DATA_DOWNLOAD_OPENHANDS_URL`) by the `author_ref` on the driver page. Three
things about it, all learned from real runs:

- **A tool-schema blip is not a failed job.** `deepseek-v4-flash` occasionally
  adds a `risk` argument to a `terminal` call; the tool's model forbids unknown
  fields, so the call is rejected with `extra_forbidden`. It is marked
  `retryable: true`, the agent recovers on the next turn (observed: within 18s,
  one occurrence in ~55 terminal calls), and the conversation still finishes.
  Nothing in the agent profile can prevent it — the schema is baked into the
  image. The harness therefore trusts the forge over the agent's exit code: if
  the branch exists at a new sha, the run counts even when the agent reported
  failure on its way out.
- **`execution_status: idle` is not "done".** It is the at-rest state, and a
  conversation starts there even when the run was requested in the same call.
  Only `finished`, `error` and `stopped` end a wait.
- **Attribution goes in `tags`, not `observability_metadata`.** The latter is
  accepted and silently dropped.
